questions.q: Which of these is **not** one of the seven characteristics of living organisms?
questions.solution:
The seven are movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion and nutrition — **MRS GREN**.

**Combustion** is burning, a chemical process that living things do not carry out.

questions.q: Which structure is found in a plant cell but not in an animal cell?
questions.solution:
The **cell wall**, made of cellulose, gives the plant cell its rigid shape and support.

Plant cells also have **chloroplasts** and a large permanent **vacuole**. All four structures listed as options are in both — only the wall is exclusive.

questions.q: Diffusion is the net movement of particles:
questions.solution:
Particles move **down** the concentration gradient, from where they are crowded to where they are not, by their own random motion.

It needs **no energy** from the cell — which is exactly what distinguishes it from active transport.

Osmosis is the diffusion of **water** through a partially permeable membrane, from a **dilute** solution (high water potential) to a **concentrated** one.

The membrane lets water through and holds the solute back — which is why only the water moves.
options: water from a dilute to a concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane
water from a concentrated to a dilute solution

questions.q: Enzymes are denatured at high temperature because:
questions.solution:
Heat breaks the weak bonds holding the protein's shape, so the **active site** no longer fits the substrate.

The change is **permanent** — cooling does not restore it, which is why a boiled egg never un-boils.

questions.q: How many levels are there in the sequence: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism?
questions.solution: $\mathbf{5}$ — each level is built from the one before, with new capabilities appearing at every step.

questions.q: How many characteristics of living organisms are there (MRS GREN)?
questions.solution: $\mathbf{7}$ — movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition.

questions.q: A cell appears $50$ mm long under a microscope, and its real length is $0.1$ mm. Find the magnification.
questions.solution:
$\text{Magnification} = \dfrac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}} = \dfrac{50}{0.1} = \mathbf{500}$.

Both measurements must be in the **same unit** before dividing — that is where this calculation usually goes wrong.

questions.q: At approximately what pH does the stomach enzyme pepsin work best?
questions.solution:
About pH $\mathbf{2}$ — strongly acidic, which is why the stomach produces hydrochloric acid.

Other enzymes have quite different optima: salivary amylase works near pH $7$ and is destroyed the moment it reaches the stomach.

questions.q: At approximately what temperature (in °C) do most human enzymes work best?
questions.solution:
About $\mathbf{37}$°C, which is body temperature — no coincidence.

Above about $40$°C the rate falls sharply as the enzymes denature, which is why a high fever is dangerous.

questions.q: Name five structures found in a plant cell and give the function of each.
questions.solution:
**Cell wall** — a rigid layer of cellulose outside the membrane. Gives support and shape, and stops the cell bursting when it takes in water.

**Cell membrane** — partially permeable; controls what enters and leaves.

**Cytoplasm** — the jelly where most chemical reactions take place.

**Nucleus** — contains the DNA and controls the cell's activities.

**Chloroplasts** — contain chlorophyll and carry out photosynthesis. Found in the green parts only, never in the roots.

**Vacuole** — a large permanent sac of cell sap. When full it presses outwards against the wall, making the cell **turgid**, and it is this pressure that holds a non-woody plant upright.

**Mitochondria** — release energy by aerobic respiration. Plants respire too, all the time.

A wilting plant is one whose vacuoles have lost water, so the cells are no longer pressing against their walls.

questions.q: Describe what happens to a plant cell and an animal cell when each is placed in pure water, and explain the difference.
questions.solution:
**Plant cell in pure water.** Water enters by osmosis and the vacuole swells, pressing the contents against the cell wall.

The cell becomes **turgid**. The strong cellulose wall resists the pressure, so the cell stops expanding and does **not** burst. Turgidity is the normal, healthy state for a plant cell.

**Animal cell in pure water.** Water enters by osmosis and the cell swells, but there is **no wall** to resist it.

The cell swells until the membrane bursts — **lysis**. A red blood cell in pure water bursts within seconds.

**The difference** is entirely the cell wall.

**In concentrated solution**, both lose water. The plant cell's membrane pulls away from the wall — **plasmolysis** — and the plant wilts, though it can often recover. The animal cell shrinks and crinkles.

**Why it matters medically:** intravenous drips must be at the **same** concentration as blood plasma. Pure water would burst the patient's red blood cells.

questions.q: What are enzymes? Explain the lock-and-key model, and describe how temperature and pH affect enzyme activity.
questions.solution:
**What they are.** Biological catalysts — proteins that speed up reactions in living things without being used up.

**Lock and key.** Each enzyme has an **active site** with a particular shape. Only a substrate of the matching shape can fit into it, which is why enzymes are so **specific** — one enzyme, usually one reaction.

The enzyme and substrate form a complex, the reaction takes place, the products leave, and the enzyme is free to start again.

**Temperature.**

• As it rises, molecules move faster, collide more often, and the rate **increases**.

• At the **optimum** (about $37$°C for human enzymes) the rate is greatest.

• Above it, the rate falls **sharply**, because heat breaks the bonds holding the protein's shape. The active site is distorted and the enzyme is **denatured** — permanently.

Note the asymmetry of the graph: the rise is gradual, the fall is a cliff. Cold enzymes are slow but unharmed; hot ones are destroyed.

**pH.** Each enzyme has an optimum — pepsin at about pH $2$, amylase near pH $7$, trypsin at about pH $8$. Away from it the shape is disturbed, and far from it the enzyme denatures.

That is why digestion needs an acidic stomach and an alkaline small intestine: different enzymes, different conditions.

questions.q: Compare diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
questions.solution:
**Diffusion** — the net movement of particles from high to low concentration, by random motion.

• **Down** the gradient

• **No energy** required

• **Example:** oxygen entering the blood in the alveoli

**Osmosis** — the diffusion of **water** through a partially permeable membrane, from a dilute to a concentrated solution.

• **Down** the water gradient

• **No energy** required

• **Example:** water entering root hair cells

**Active transport** — movement of particles **against** the concentration gradient, using a carrier protein.

• **Up** the gradient

• **Energy required**, from respiration (ATP)

• **Example:** mineral ions taken into root hairs from very dilute soil water; glucose reabsorbed in the kidney

**The test that separates them:** a cell poisoned so that it cannot respire continues to take up substances by diffusion and osmosis, but active transport stops at once.

Diffusion is rolling downhill; active transport is pushing uphill, and pushing costs.

questions.q: Explain why large organisms need specialised exchange surfaces, while a single-celled organism does not.
questions.solution:
**The problem.** As anything grows, its **volume** increases faster than its **surface area**.

Double every length and the surface area becomes $4$ times larger, while the volume becomes $8$ times larger. The **surface area to volume ratio therefore falls**.

**Why that matters.** The volume decides how much oxygen the organism needs and how much waste it makes. The surface decides how fast those can be exchanged.

**A single-celled organism** such as Amoeba has an enormous surface area for its tiny volume, and no part of it is far from the outside. Diffusion across the membrane is entirely sufficient.

**A large organism** has far too little surface for its bulk, and its inner cells are many centimetres from the outside — a distance diffusion cannot cover in any useful time.

**The solution — specialised exchange surfaces**, all of them built to the same recipe:

• **Large surface area** — alveoli, villi, root hairs, gill filaments

• **Thin** — one cell thick, so the diffusion distance is short

• **Good blood supply** — to keep the concentration gradient steep

• **Moist**, since gases must dissolve to cross

Plus a **transport system** to carry substances the rest of the way. Human lungs pack about $80$ m$^{2}$ of surface into a chest a few litres in volume — the whole design is an answer to a problem of geometry.
